EAQ2.brief: The sky gives a base color to everything below it, so it has a strong effect on the mood of a scene. Unreal offers two common ways to make a sky. One is the atmosphere system, which calculates the sky from a sun light. The other is an HDRI, a 360 degree photo of a real sky that also lights the scene. In this quest you light the same scene both ways and compare which one fits a mood you chose better.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Write one line that describes the mood you want, for example a cold, foggy morning or a warm sunset. If you already have a mood target picture, use that. Create a new level with File, New Level, Empty Level, and place a floor and a few objects in it.
Light the scene with Sky Atmosphere, a Directional Light (the sun), a Sky Light (soft light that comes from the whole sky), and Height Fog.

Duplicate the level and light the copy with an HDRI instead. You can use the HDRI Backdrop actor, which needs the HDRI Backdrop plugin from Edit > Plugins and comes with a sample HDRI, or a Sky Light with a cubemap, which is a texture that covers all directions.
Push each version toward your mood. Change the sun angle, the fog color and the fog density until the mood is close.
Compare the two versions from the same camera bookmark, so that both pictures show exactly the same view.
EAQ2.done_when: Send side-by-side screenshots of the atmosphere version and the HDRI version taken from the same bookmark. Add your one-line mood, and 2 lines that say which version fits it better.

checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a room level of your own, or build a simple closed room in a new level from cubes: a floor, four walls and a ceiling. Set the exposure to a fixed value: add a Post Process Volume, tick Infinite Extent (Unbound), and set Metering Mode to Manual in its Exposure section. Exposure is how bright the camera makes the picture, and a fixed value stops Unreal from adjusting it, so you can see brightness changes.
Place 2 lights and give them real-world intensities, in candela or lumens, and a realistic color temperature.

Apply an IES profile to one of the lights. Lamp makers offer IES files as free downloads on their websites. Drag one .ies file into the Content Browser to import it, then pick it in the IES Texture setting of the light. Compare how the light looks with the profile and without it.
Write down the intensity and the temperature you used, and where you got each value from.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any level that has a few objects in it: the level of the template works, and so does a scene of your own. Save 3 camera bookmarks: one wide view, one medium view and one detail view.
Place a Cine Camera Actor and set its focal length and focus distance. Then pilot the camera, which means you look through it and move it, and frame the best view.
Turn on a composition overlay, such as the rule of thirds grid or a similar one. Use it to adjust the frame.
Take a High Resolution Screenshot while you look through the Cine Camera.

EAQ12.brief: A diorama is a small, complete scene, like a model in a box. A small finished scene teaches you more than a big scene that you never finish, because you have to make every part work together. In this quest you combine several skills: you build a small piece of landscape with plants, light it toward a mood you chose, and take three still images. Everything you need to build is listed in the steps.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Choose a mood target: one reference picture, or three lines that give the time of day, the color of the main light and the feeling you want. Then build a small diorama of roughly 10 x 10 m in a new level: create a small Landscape in Landscape Mode, sculpt it a little, and paint a few plants or rocks on it in Foliage Mode. You can reuse a terrain of your own.

Light it toward your mood target. Add a Directional Light, a Sky Light, a Sky Atmosphere and Height Fog, and at least one local light, such as a Point Light, with an intensity that you set in real units (candela or lumens).

Set the exposure and the post process settings on purpose, so that the result is your choice and not the default: add a Post Process Volume, tick Infinite Extent (Unbound), and set Metering Mode to Manual in its Exposure section.
Save 3 camera bookmarks and take a still from each. Take one of them through a Cine Camera Actor: place one, right-click it and choose Pilot, frame the view, and take a High Resolution Screenshot.
Write 3 lines that say what matches the target and what does not match it yet.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level of your own that has a dark room with a window, or build one in a new Basic level from cubes: a floor, four walls and a ceiling, with a gap in one wall as the window. Select the Exponential Height Fog actor in the level. If there is none, drag one in from the Place Actors panel, under Visual Effects. In the Details panel, turn on Volumetric Fog. Aim a Directional Light or a Spot Light through the window into the room, and adjust the scene until you can see light shafts coming through the window.
Select the light and change Volumetric Scattering Intensity in its Details panel, which controls how strongly that light shows in the fog. The shafts should support the image and not wash it out.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any outdoor level with a main subject in front and something far behind it: the level of the template works, and so does a scene of your own. In the Place Actors panel, search for Local Fog Volume and drag 2 of them into the level. Scale and move them so that they separate the foreground from the background, for example one behind the main subject and one far away. Change the two Extinction values in the Details panel to make the fog thicker or thinner.
Take one screenshot with the volumes and one screenshot without them, from the same view.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any outdoor level that has a Directional Light and a few objects that cast shadows: the level of the template works. Render the same view at 3 sun angles and with 2 Source Angle values for each, so that you get 6 renders. Select the Directional Light and rotate it to change the sun angle. Source Angle is in its Details panel, under Light: a small value gives sharp shadows and a large value gives soft shadows. Take each render from the same camera bookmark.
Pick the render where the shapes are the easiest to read, and write one line that says why.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a material named M_Basic in the folder UC/Materials (create the folder if it does not exist yet). Double-click it to open the Material Editor.
Add a Constant3Vector node, which holds a color, and connect it to Base Color. Add Constant nodes, which each hold one number, and connect them to Roughness and Metallic.
Look at the material in the preview viewport. Open the Stats panel to see the instruction counts, which show how much work the material costs to draw.
Apply the material to a mesh in any level, for example a cube or a sphere from the Place Actors panel.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Make 4 swatches, each a simple material on its own sphere: a rough dielectric, a glossy dielectric, a rough metal and a polished metal.
Keep the Base Color values of each swatch in a plausible range. Do not use pure black or pure white.

Add a normal map to one swatch. A normal map is a texture that fakes small bumps on the surface. The Textures folder of the Starter Content has normal maps, with names that end in _N. Compare the swatch with and without it.

Place the four spheres next to each other in one level, so that they are all under the same light. The level of the template works, and so does a lit scene of your own. Put a Text Render actor at each sphere as a label.

EAQ15.brief: Most materials get their detail from textures, which are images that the material reads, or samples. UVs are the coordinates that say which part of the image goes on which part of the mesh. Wrong texture settings are a common problem because Unreal does not show an error, the surface just looks a little wrong. In this quest you take three textures, check their settings, and use them in a material with adjustable tiling.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Pick a color texture, a normal texture and a packed texture of the same surface. In the Textures folder of the Starter Content, color textures end in _D, normal textures in _N and packed mask textures in _M. You can also import your own files. A packed texture stores a different grayscale map in each color channel. Open each texture and check its sRGB setting and its compression settings.
Create a material named M_Surface and sample the three textures in it. Add a TexCoord node with a tiling parameter, so that you can change how many times the texture repeats.
Split the packed texture into its channels, so that you can use each channel on its own.
Apply the material to a large mesh, such as a cube scaled into a floor. Find one place where you can see the texture repeat. Fix it by changing the scale or by rotating the UVs.

EAQ16.brief: A parameter is a value in a material that has a name and can be changed later without opening the material graph. A Material Instance is a copy of a material that only changes those parameters. This lets one material serve many different surfaces. In this quest you build a material with parameters and create three instances that look different from each other.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Create a material named M_Surface that reads a color texture and a normal texture from the Starter Content, or start from a textured material of your own. Give it scalar parameters (single numbers, for example for roughness and tiling), vector parameters (colors, for example a tint) and texture parameters.
Put the parameters in named groups. Give each one a sensible default value and a sort priority, which sets the order they are listed in.
Create 3 instances of the material that look like different materials.

EAQ17.brief: A landscape is the large terrain actor that Unreal uses for outdoor ground, and the ground is most of what you see outside. A landscape material holds several layers, such as grass, dirt and rock, and you paint these layers onto the terrain with a brush. In this quest you build a landscape material with three layers and paint all of them on a landscape.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Build a landscape material that has 3 layers. Use a Landscape Layer Blend node, which is the node that mixes the layers based on where you paint. For the layers you can use textures from the Starter Content, such as grass, rock and ground.

Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level, open Landscape Mode and choose New on the Manage tab. Assign your material to the landscape. Create the layer info objects, which are small assets that store where each layer is painted. Then paint all 3 layers on the landscape.
Stand at the height of a player and look at the ground. Keep the tiling scale sensible, so that the texture is not too large and not too small from there.
Create a decal material. To do this, set the Material Domain of the material to Deferred Decal.

Open any level with a floor and walls: the level of the Third Person template works, and so does a scene of your own. Place 3 decals in it: one of grime, one stain, and one directional marker such as an arrow.
Look at each decal from a low angle and check if it looks stretched. If it does, fix the size of the decal box, which is the box that shows how far the decal projects.

EAQ24.brief: A scene that you walk through at eye level shows problems that a still render hides, such as gaps, stretched textures and places where you get stuck. A master material is one material with many parameters, and the surfaces in the scene use instances of it. In this quest you make a small scene walkable, build one master material for its surfaces, and fix what looks wrong when you walk around. Everything you need to build is listed in the steps.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template with Starter Content, or create one. Use a small scene of your own, or build a diorama of roughly 10 x 10 m in a new level: a small Landscape, a few meshes such as rocks and walls, and basic lighting. Make it walkable: add a Player Start, make sure the meshes have collision so that you cannot walk through them, and leave no dead ends.
Build one master material named M_Master_Surface with parameters for color, roughness, a texture and tiling. Put its parameters in named groups in the Details panel of each parameter.
Use instances of this material on at least 5 surfaces in the scene.

Build a landscape material with 3 layers that uses a Landscape Layer Blend node, and paint the layers on the landscape. Place at least 3 decals that each have a purpose, such as a stain under a pipe or an arrow toward the path. A decal is a material with its Material Domain set to Deferred Decal.
Walk through the scene in PIE, which means Play In Editor. Fix anything that looks wrong at eye level.
Write a short note that lists the parameters of the master material and says what each one is for.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Place three cubes in any level and scale them to different sizes as blockout meshes. Pick any texture from the Starter Content. Make a material that uses a world-aligned texture: add the WorldAlignedTexture node, connect a Texture Object node with your texture to its TextureObject input, and connect its XYZ Texture output to Base Color. Apply the material to blockout meshes that you have scaled to different sizes. The pattern keeps the same size on all of them.

Make a second material that uses a normal Texture Sample node, which follows the UVs of the mesh. Apply it to the same meshes, and compare the two results. Look at how the pattern stretches on the scaled meshes.

EAQ20.brief: Placing grass by hand over a large landscape takes a long time. A landscape material can place grass meshes for you, on every spot where one paint layer is painted. In this quest you connect grass to one layer and check that the grass follows your painting.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. You need a Landscape with a landscape material that has at least two paint layers. If you have none, create a new level, make a Landscape in Landscape Mode, and build a material with a Landscape Layer Blend node that has two layers, such as Grass and Dirt. You also need a Landscape Grass Type asset: right-click in the Content Browser, open Foliage, choose Landscape Grass Type, and add any small mesh to it, such as the bush from the Starter Content. In the landscape material, add a Landscape Grass Output node. Select it, add one element under Grass Types in the Details panel, and pick your Landscape Grass Type asset. Add a Landscape Layer Sample node, type the name of one paint layer in its Parameter Name, and connect it to the input of the grass type. Now that one paint layer controls where the grass appears.
Paint that layer on the landscape. Confirm that grass appears only in the places you painted.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in a dark place, such as a closed room built from cubes, so that the glow is easy to see. Use a flat cube or a plane as the screen. Make an emissive screen or sign. In its material, multiply a color or a texture by a Scalar Parameter named Intensity and connect the result to Emissive Color. Make a Material Instance, so that you can change how strong the glow is, and try the values 1, 10 and 50.
With Lumen on, check how much the glow lights the surfaces near it. Work out in which cases you would still need a real light.

EAQ25.brief: A Static Switch Parameter is an on or off switch in a material that turns a part of the graph on or off for each instance. Switches are cheap for one instance, but every different combination makes Unreal compile another version of the shader, called a shader permutation. Too many permutations make compile times and memory use grow. In this quest you add switches to a master material, count the permutations, and remove a switch that is not worth its cost.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a master material of your own, or make a small one now: a material named M_Master_Surface with a color texture, a normal texture and a roughness parameter. Extend it with Static Switch Parameters: one that turns a detail normal on or off, one for emissive, and one more of your choice.
Create instances that use different combinations of the switches.
Write down how many shader permutations your switches can create.
Remove one switch that is not worth its cost, and explain why you removed it.

EAQ26.brief: A Material Function is a small piece of material graph that you save as its own asset and can use in many materials. It stops you from building the same group of nodes again and again, and when you fix the function, every material that uses it is fixed too. In this quest you move one part of a material into a function and use it in two materials.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a material of your own, or make a small one with a color texture and a normal texture. In it, build detail normal blending: sample a second normal texture with a higher tiling and combine it with the first one using the BlendAngleCorrectedNormals node. This is a group of nodes you would repeat in many materials. Move it into a Material Function named MF_DetailNormal.
Give the function inputs with clear names and default values. Also write a description for it.
Use the function in 2 different materials.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Make a material with two surfaces, for example stone as the base and moss on top, using textures from the Starter Content. Add a Vertex Color node and use its red channel as the Alpha of a Lerp node between the two surfaces, so that red paint puts the second surface over the base surface.

Place a mesh with enough vertices in the level, for example a sphere, and apply the material. The paint is stored on the vertices, so a simple cube has too few. Use Mesh Paint mode to paint on the mesh.
Add a height-based blend, which uses a height texture to decide where the second surface appears first. This makes the edge look sharp and natural and not like a soft smear.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick a high-poly mesh, which is a mesh with a very large number of triangles. If you have none, use the most detailed mesh in your project, or make a sphere in Modeling Mode with a very high subdivision level. Enable Nanite on it: open the mesh and tick Enable Nanite Support in its Nanite Settings. Inspect it in the level with the Nanite visualization modes Triangles, Clusters and Overdraw.
On the Nanite documentation page linked on this quest, read the list of things that Nanite does not support. Note which kinds of materials in a project would be affected, such as translucent ones.
Try Nanite displacement on one mesh if your engine version and your project support it. If they do not, write what you would need to enable.
Write 3 lines: when you would use Nanite, when you would not use it, and one cost to watch.

EAQ29.brief: The eye of a viewer goes first to the brightest spot with the most contrast. A hero area is the most important place in a scene, the place you want people to look at. Lighting artists often use three lights for it: the key light is the main light, the fill light softens the shadows, and the rim light comes from behind to separate the subject from the background. In this quest you light one hero area on purpose, check what the extra lights cost, and ask another person where they look first.
EAQ29.done_when: Send before and after stills taken from the same Cine Camera, the stat numbers, and the comment from the person you asked.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any level with a few objects in it: the level of the template works, and so does a scene of your own. Place a Cine Camera Actor that frames the scene and take a still through it before you change anything. Pick one hero area. It can be an entrance, a landmark, or a focal prop (the object the viewer should notice).
Set the direction of the key, fill and rim light on purpose. Use physical units for all of them.
Check the Lumen reflections and the GI (global illumination, which is bounced light) in the area. Use the Lumen visualization modes for this.
Run the console command stat unit before and after you add your lights. It shows how long each frame takes. Note the cost of your extra lights.
Ask one other person, such as another learner or a friend, to look at the image and say where their eye goes first.

EAQ30.brief: Color grading means changing the colors and contrast of the final image, like editing a photo. In Unreal you do this in a Post Process Volume. A LUT (lookup table) is a small texture that stores a color grade made in an image editor, so that you can apply it in the engine. Grading finishes an image, but it cannot fix bad lighting. In this quest you grade a scene by hand, grade it again with a LUT, and compare the two.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any lit level: the level of the template works, and so does a scene of your own. Save a camera bookmark and take one screenshot without any grade. Then grade the scene in a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on. Start with the white balance, then change the global settings, and then the shadows, midtones and highlights.

Now grade with a LUT. Take a screenshot of the scene without a grade. Download the neutral LUT image, a LUT that changes nothing yet (256 x 16 pixels), from the Epic documentation page about color grading with Look-Up Tables. Open both in an image editor, apply the same color adjustments to the screenshot and to the LUT image, and save the LUT image. Import it into Unreal, open the texture, and set Texture Group to ColorLookupTable and Mip Gen Settings to NoMipmaps. In the Post Process Volume, open Color Grading, then Misc, and assign it as the Color Grading LUT.
Compare the manual grade with the LUT grade.
Keep one screenshot without any grade for reference.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Work in any lit level: the level of the template works, and so does a scene of your own. Place a Cine Camera Actor and frame a view. Create a Level Sequence that is one frame long, add the Cine Camera to it, and make sure it has a Camera Cut track so that the render uses this camera.
Render it with Movie Render Queue. Use anti-aliasing samples, which smooth jagged edges by rendering the frame several times, and choose a high resolution.
Save the render settings as a preset, so that you can use them again later.
Take a High Resolution Screenshot of the same frame and compare it with the render.

EAQ35.brief: A reference scene is a neutral level with known lighting that people use to check their assets. When everyone on a team puts an asset into the same scene, everyone judges it under the same light, so the results can be compared. In this quest you build such a scene, write a short guide for it, and show it to a mentor. Everything you need to build is listed in the steps.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. In a new level, build a scene that other people can drop assets into to check them. Include neutral props, a pair of balls (one gray and one chrome), and a Macbeth-style swatch board, which is a board of standard color patches.

Light the scene with physical units and a fixed exposure (a Post Process Volume with Metering Mode set to Manual). Give it a hero area, the place where the asset stands, with a key light, a fill light and a rim light.

Build the surfaces of the scene from one master material with instances. Use at least one Material Function in it, and put one vertex-painted blend on a prop, which is a second surface that you paint on in Mesh Paint mode.
Provide 3 Cine Cameras with a camera bookmark at each one, and a Movie Render Queue preset: a saved set of render settings for a one-frame Level Sequence.
Write a README of one page. It must say how to use the scene, what the exposure is, and what people should not change.
Record a short video clip (30 seconds or less) in which you put one asset into the scene and look at it through the three cameras.
EAQ35.done_when: Send your README as text, a screenshot from each of the 3 cameras, a screenshot of the Movie Render Queue preset, and the short video clip. A mentor reviews your work and checks that the scene could be used with only your README.

checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level and make a Landscape in Landscape Mode. Decide where a path runs across it. Make a PCG graph that scatters debris or rocks on the surface. Enable the Procedural Content Generation Framework (PCG) plugin in Edit > Plugins if it is off. Right-click in the Content Browser, open PCG and choose PCG Graph. In the graph, connect a Get Landscape Data node to a Surface Sampler node and then to a Static Mesh Spawner node, and pick a mesh under Mesh Entries, for example the rock from the Starter Content. Place a PCG Volume in the level, set Graph on its PCG component, and click Generate.

Add one rule to the graph that keeps the paths clear. It can be a density rule, which controls how many objects appear, for example a Density Filter node after the Surface Sampler. It can also be an exclusion rule, which removes objects from an area, for example a Difference node that subtracts the points near a spline along the path.

EAQ33.brief: The Water system is a plugin in Unreal that gives you ready-made lakes, rivers and oceans. Water reflects everything around it, so its color and clarity have a strong effect on the mood of a scene. In this quest you add a small water body and adjust it until it fits a mood you chose.
EAQ33.done_when: Send a still image of the water, and the one line that describes the mood you aimed for.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level and make a Landscape in Landscape Mode. Write one line that says which mood the water should have, for example clear and tropical, or dark and murky. Add a small lake or a river with the Water system. Enable the Water plugin in Edit > Plugins and restart the editor. Then search for Water Body in the Place Actors panel and drag a Water Body Lake or a Water Body River into the level.

Tune the color and the scattering of the water until it matches your mood. Select the water body and find Water Material in its Details panel. Make a copy of that Material Instance, assign the copy, and change its Absorption and Scattering values. Scattering controls how light spreads inside the water, which changes how clear or murky it looks.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open a level of your own that has a Landscape, or create a new level and make a Landscape in Landscape Mode. Set up a Procedural Foliage Volume with 2 species. First open Edit > Editor Preferences, find the Experimental section and enable Procedural Foliage. Right-click in the Content Browser, open Foliage, and create two Static Mesh Foliage assets (one per species) and one Procedural Foliage Spawner. Give each Static Mesh Foliage asset a mesh, for example a tree of your own, or the bush and the rock from the Starter Content. Open the spawner and add both species under Foliage Types. Drag the spawner into the level, scale it over the area where the forest edge should be, and click Resimulate in its Details panel.

Tune the spacing settings in the two Static Mesh Foliage assets, such as Shade Radius, Initial Seed Density and Average Spread Distance, and click Resimulate after each change. Continue until the edge of the forest looks natural and not uniform.
Read the Gameplay Ability System overview page in the Unreal Engine documentation. You can skip the code samples if you like.
Write a one-line definition for each of these five terms: Ability System Component, Gameplay Ability, Attribute, Gameplay Effect, and Gameplay Tag.
Pick a mechanic from a game you know, such as a dash, a heal or a stun. Describe how it works using those five terms.
Name one thing in a game level that could apply a Gameplay Effect, for example a hazard, a pickup or a zone.

EAQ22.brief: Players look first at the brightest part of the screen and at the places with the most contrast. This means lighting is a tool for guiding the player, not only for making a level look good. In this quest you do one lighting pass on a level with pickups, so that the pickups and the way to them are easy to see.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level of your own that has pickups to collect. If you have none, create a new level with File, New Level, Empty Level, build two or three rooms from cubes with one dead end, and place three small spheres as pickups. Move the camera to the view the player has at the start, and save a camera bookmark there (Ctrl plus a number key). Take the before screenshot now.
Set up the basic lighting with the Env. Light Mixer window. Use it to add a Directional Light, a Sky Light, a Sky Atmosphere and Height Fog.
Make each pickup stand out. You can put a small Point Light on it, or you can place the pickup in the brightest area.
Make the dead ends darker or less noticeable, so that the player sees the route to the pickups first.

Add a Post Process Volume and turn on Infinite Extent so that it affects the whole level. Then bring the minimum and maximum values of the auto exposure closer together, so that the brightness does not jump when the player moves between rooms.

GDQ5.done_when: Send a short video clip (30 seconds or less), or two or three screenshots, taken while playing in the editor, that show you collecting all 3 coins and the win message appearing. Also send a screenshot of the AddCoin function.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Create a Blueprint named BP_UUGameMode as a child of the GameMode of the template: right-click the GameMode Blueprint of the template in the Content Browser and choose Create Child Blueprint Class. Give it an Integer variable named Collected, and an Integer variable named Target that is set to 3. Then set BP_UUGameMode as the GameMode Override of the level in World Settings.

Make a Blueprint named BP_Coin with a mesh and a Sphere Collision. In its On Component Begin Overlap event, compare Other Actor with Get Player Pawn and use a Branch, so that the coin only reacts to the player. Then use Get Game Mode, then Cast to BP_UUGameMode, then call a function named AddCoin, and after that call Destroy Actor.
Inside the AddCoin function, add 1 to Collected. Then use a Branch node that checks whether Collected >= Target.
On the True output of the Branch, show a win message. A Print String node is enough, and a widget on screen is a bonus.
Place 3 coins in the level in spots where the player has to move around to reach them. Play in the editor (PIE) until you win.

EAQ23.brief: A master material is one material built with parameters, which are values such as a color or a roughness that you leave open to change. From it you make Material Instances, which are light copies that only change those parameters. This way one material can give many objects different looks. In this quest you build a small master material and three instances, and use their colors to show the player what each object in a level is for.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a new material named M_UC_Master in the folder /Content/UC/Materials (create the folder if it does not exist yet).

Add these parameters to it: a Vector parameter named BaseColor, two Scalar parameters named Roughness and Metallic, and a Scalar parameter named EmissiveStrength. Multiply EmissiveStrength by the color and connect the result to the Emissive input.
Give every parameter a Group in its Details panel. Groups keep the parameter list tidy when you open an instance.
Make 3 Material Instances from it: MI_Gameplay_Interact (bright, with a little emissive glow), MI_Gameplay_Hazard (red), and MI_Gameplay_Neutral (matte gray).

Apply the instances to three objects in a level: one that the player can use, one that is a hazard, and one that is only scenery. If your level has no such objects, place three cubes that stand for them. Players should be able to tell the role of each object by its color.
